analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical injury lawsuits at $250,000 and shields FDA-approved drugs from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 12, 2003 and placed on the Senate calendar, the bill never reached a floor vote and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for every medical malpractice lawsuit in the country. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how severe the injury, shortened the deadlines for suing, limited lawyers' fees, made it much harder to win punitive damages, and barred punitive damages entirely against drugs and devices approved by the FDA. It also would have overridden any state law that gave injured patients more generous protections.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and insurers would benefit from predictable, capped liability, since the bill's stated purpose was to lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine.' Drug and device makers would gain the most protection: no punitive damages for FDA-approved products, and doctors who prescribe those products could not even be named in the lawsuit. Patients who win lawsuits would keep unlimited recovery for actual financial losses and would pay lower lawyer fees under the bill's sliding-scale fee cap.

how_it_helps.text: It leaves recovery of full economic damages — medical bills and lost earnings — completely unlimited [S3].

It caps noneconomic damages (pain, suffering, disfigurement) at $250,000 per injury, which supporters argued would lower malpractice insurance premiums and reduce 'defensive medicine' that drives up health costs [S2] [S3].
It caps lawyer contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000), so injured patients keep a larger share of any award [S3].
It bars punitive damages against drug and device makers whose products complied with FDA approval, and shields prescribing doctors from product-liability suits over approved drugs [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients catastrophically injured by medical negligence would bear the cost. The $250,000 cap applies regardless of how many defendants or claims are involved, and it hits hardest those with little measurable economic loss — children, retirees, and people not in the workforce — for whom pain and suffering is nearly the whole claim. Damages would also be reduced by any insurance or benefit payments the patient already received, lawsuits would face shorter filing deadlines, punitive damages would require clear-and-convincing proof of malicious intent, and no state could keep or adopt more generous rules.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages applies regardless of the severity of the injury or the number of defendants, so a patient left permanently disabled with low documented earnings would face the same ceiling as a minor injury [S3].
The bill preempts state laws that provide greater damages or longer filing periods, overriding protections states had chosen for their own residents [S2] [S3].

Punitive damages would be unavailable against an FDA-approved drug even where state law allowed them, unless the manufacturer knowingly misled the FDA — even as the bill's own findings cite the liability system as the main cost driver [S2] [S3].

Supporters' good-faith case — that malpractice premiums were restricting access to care — rests on findings in the bill itself, but independent evidence that caps reliably lower patients' health costs was not part of the record provided [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flowed mostly to defendants: malpractice insurers got capped payouts, providers got predictable exposure, and drug makers got immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved products. The people who actually bore medical harm paid for those gains through lower recoveries and shorter deadlines. Its one clear benefit to patients — unlimited economic damages and lower lawyer fees — was real but secondary, and the preemption of state law meant patients in states with stronger protections would lose them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar within a day, and then simply sat there — no committee action, no debate, no vote — until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. John Ensign introduced the bill on March 12, 2003, with six Republican cosponsors [S1] [S3].
By March 13, 2003 it had been read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 33 — the list of bills awaiting floor consideration [S5].

The action history shows no committee referral, no floor debate, and no vote after that placement; the bill's last recorded action is from March 2003, and it expired when the 108th Congress ended January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by medical negligence kept the full remedies their state laws provide, since no caps, deadlines, or FDA shield took effect. Malpractice insurers, providers, and drug makers did not get the liability protections the bill would have given them.

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Introduced the HEALTH Act of 2003 on March 12, 2003

for.name: 7 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Gregg, Enzi, Thomas, Voinovich, and Kyl
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction

against.name: Senate leadership of both parties
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up for debate or a vote despite its placement on the calendar in March 2003

against.name: Opponents of federal malpractice caps
against.role: Coalition of Senate Democrats, trial lawyers, and patient advocates during the 2003–2004 malpractice debate
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed federal caps on malpractice damages, and a Senate attempt to move a similar malpractice cap bill failed to clear a procedural vote requiring 60 senators in April 2003

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Republicans, and medical liability reform was a Republican priority in the 108th Congress; no Democrat sponsored the bill, and it never came to a vote that would have shown the full split.

industries.note: Caps on pain-and-suffering awards and damages reduced by insurance benefits would directly shrink the claims insurers pay. Their gain comes out of the compensation owed to injured patients.

No punitive damages for FDA-approved products, and stricter filing rules for punitive claims, would sharply limit the largest verdicts against them. The exception applies only if a company knowingly misled the FDA.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other health care providers
industries.note: Providers would gain capped liability, protection from punitive damages, and immunity from suits over FDA-approved drugs they prescribe — and supporters argued lower premiums keep doctors practicing, including in high-risk specialties. The cost falls on patients who can no longer recover full compensation from them.
Sliding-scale contingency fee caps and the $250,000 damage cap would cut both lawyers' fees and their clients' recoveries. Their opposition ran alongside injured patients' interests in this bill.
